body_markdown:
Context can mean everything. I go to many different kinds of car shows: weekend shows, cruise-ins, Concours d’Elegance, and I love them all. But when you see a car at a monthly cruise night that you’d generally only see at a very high-end show, it makes the sighting all the more special.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


And such was the case at the May Classy Chassy car club cruise night at Coral Ridge Mall, in Coralville, Iowa. This is always a nice show, and I have seen and documented some very neat stuff here. But that good luck—plus the fact I have been going to this show with my uncle, Dave Klockau, since about 2005—still didn’t prepare me for this vision in Gauguin Red.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


I just went nuts when I saw it. A genuine classic—one of those gorgeous, rare, powerful cars that you just don’t see outside of classic car coffee table books and prestigious shows. I just know Jay Leno must have one! I have seen one of these relatively recently; last year there was one at the Geneva Concours d’Elegance, “The Pebble Beach of the Midwest,” as my friend Jim Smith (who has been a judge at the event the last two years) and I affectionately call it.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


And at the recent Geneva show last year, as I was walking around with Jim, we came upon a gorgeous ’57 300C in black with saddle tan leather. As I recall, it was still with the man who bought it new, and we spent a happy few minutes chatting with him.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


But you see, that was a Concours d’Elegance, with a magnificent Mercedes 540K, a Maybach, a Citroën DS, and more. So, despite how wonderful it is to see a 300C anywhere, it was even more special seeing this fantastic red example at a monthly cruise night, among the Mustangs, Chevelle SSs, Chevy C10s and VW Beetles.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


Anyway, enough panting and gushing—let’s get to our subject! The 300 Letter Series are considered amazing vehicles by most everyone, and they’re truly special. And the 300C of 1957 is arguably the prettiest of them all—though the 1958 300D was virtually identical.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


This was the third year of the Chrysler 300, the original arriving in 1955 and the ’56 adding a ‘B’ suffix to the name, establishing an ID pattern that would continue through 1965, when the last of the traditional Letter Series cars were produced.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


Special features included limited exterior chrome (for Detroit, for 1957) with really just the grille, taillight trim, window trim, and an abbreviated spear on the rear quarters encasing the red, white, and blue 300 logo. All cars got a full leather interior, special ducting below the headlamps for additional brake cooling, and a 392-CID V-8 with 4.0 x 3.9 bore and stroke, 9.25:1 compression ratio, and producing 375 hp at 5200 rpm along with 420 lb-ft of torque.


Thomas Klockau


And there was a reason these were called “the banker’s hot rod.” This was a strictly first-cabin automobile. While technically considered a part of the New Yorker series, it really was in a class by itself. First of all, it was regally priced at $4929 for the two-door hardtop and $5359 for the convertible. Of those, 1918 coupes and 484 convertibles were built for the model year.


Thomas Klockau


In comparison, a 1957 New Yorker two-door hardtop was priced at $4202, much less than the 300C but still clearly a premium product. A new 1957 Chevy Bel Air Sport Coupe, that darling of collectors for decades, was only $2399 with the V-8. So basically the 300C cost two ’57 Bel Airs, plus another couple hundred bucks on top for good measure.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


Despite its 126-inch wheelbase and 219.2″ overall length, a 300C would have happily stomped a ’57 Corvette in a “flying mile,” which would have been an impressive feat back then. Then you’d step out of your high-octane luxury car and walk into a supper club for a martini and surf and turf. I dig that.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


Oh, and did I mention colors? I think this Gauguin Red is my favorite color on these cars. It is such a bright, vivid color, with just a touch of coral in its hue. And contrasted with the saddle tan leather interior? Marvelous!


Thomas Klockau


Chrysler didn’t mince words in introducing the 300C to prospects. As the brochure said, “The glamour, the glory, the get-up-and-GO of the famous Chrysler 300 and the Chrysler 300 B which created such a furor in racing and sports car circles in 1955 and 1956, assume even greater stature and *exclusiveness* in their brilliant successor for 1957 – the inimitable Chrysler 300 C.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


“The 300 C FirePower V8 Engine, one of the finest, most efficient engines ever designed, develops 375 horsepower at 5200 rpm. It has two 4-barrel carburetors, a full race camshaft, mechanical valve lifters, adjustable valve rockers, heavy-duty crankshaft, double valve springs, Tri-metal main and rod bearings, and extra-deep valve seat inserts.”


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


Also per the brochure specifications, “Opt. 390 hp engine available at extra cost as part of Optional Chassis Package.” Said package also included a 10:1 compression ratio, limited-slip differential, low-backpressure exhaust system, and a high-speed camshaft. You know, just in case 375 horsepower was a tad slow for you.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


Other available 1957 Chrysler colors included Seafoam Aqua, Parade Green, Crocus Yellow, Copper Glow, Saturn Blue, Indian Turquoise, Sunset Rose, and Shell Pink. Though I seriously doubt many Shell Pink 300Cs were made! But regardless, your 300C would have any interior color you wanted, as long as it was the natural-hued leather in tan.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


Some of the swagger and speed of these gorgeous classics were revived with the new Chrysler 300 series in 2005. Sadly, those modern classic luxury sedans were stricken from the lineup a couple of years ago, leaving the sole Chrysler offering…a minivan.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


I, for one, am hoping the ghost of Walter P. Chrysler will haunt Stellantis executives until this glaring error is corrected. We need modern, classy, Chrysler sedans! Preferably with a V-6 or V-8.


My uncle is on the left, catching the 300C’s interior features.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


Until that day, all we can do is celebrate the stunning classic Chryslers of the past. Until next time, remember: if you find yourself in a supper club, you can’t go wrong with an Old Fashioned and surf and turf. And always tip your bartender!


Thomas Klockau
